name: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park
blurb: A no-fishing reserve of seagrass, mangrove and reef, with groupers, conch and sharks.

tip.title: Lose the grouper
tip.text: Nassau grouper are critically endangered and easy to overfish. Remove them and watch lionfish, lobster and reef sharks shift.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Exuma Cays Land and Sea Park

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: Seagrass meadows shelter young fish and many small invertebrates. Turtles, parrotfish and sea urchins graze them, and dead leaves become detritus.

nodes.name: Green macroalgae
nodes.desc: Calcified green algae on sand flats and reefs, grazed by conch, turtles and parrotfish.
Mangroves cover much of the park. Their prop roots shelter young reef animals such as juvenile spiny lobsters before they move to the reef.
Scrapes algae from dead coral. It is very important on Caribbean reefs because of how abundant it is.
Adults mostly graze seagrass and algae in shallow lagoons and bays. Juveniles also eat animals.
Eats mollusks, crustaceans, worms and dead animals. Juveniles settle among algae, seagrass and mangrove roots.
A reef predator of fish and small crustaceans. Spawning gatherings make it easy to overfish, and it is critically endangered.
An invasive predator of small fish and crustaceans, established across the Bahamas. Few predators are known to eat it.
A fish-eating raptor, the only animal allowed to fish in the park.
One of the largest reef predators. It eats reef fish, cephalopods and rays, and is protected in the Bahamas.
A large shark that preys on adult green turtles, among other prey.
Strong sun on clear, shallow water powers seagrass, algae and mangroves.
Shallow, sandy soil over limestone supports low coastal scrub.
Break down dead seagrass, algae, leaf litter and carcasses into nutrients.
